newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus' Clerides faces tough test in negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus' Clerides faces tough test in negotiations.

text.p: Glafcos Clerides inherited one of the toughest nuts to crack in world diplomacy when he narrowly won election as fourth president of Cyprus in 1993.

Veteran right-winger Clerides, now 78, promised to try to do away with the barbed wire that has divided Greek and Turkish Cypriots for more than two decades when he edged out millionaire George Vassiliou. The presidency had eluded him twice before.

But so far he has failed to reunite the island as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation, just as his predecessors did -- and the small army of international mediators who have been coming and going since 1974.
That was the year Turkish troops landed in Cyprus, citing their rights as a guarantor power to restore order.
The invasion followed a brief, abortive coup by Greek Cypriots who wanted union with Greece, where the military rulers at the time had engineered the toppling of the Cypriot government.
The coup collapsed but the Turkish forces remained, holding the northern third of the island.

Clerides, a dominant figure in local politics since Cyprus gained independence from Britain in 1960, is widely acknowledged to be the best match for Rauf Denktash, the veteran Turkish Cypriot leader and a fierce defender of his community's independence.
"He is trying to sell me raki in a whisky bottle," Clerides once said of the Turkish Cypriot leader, referring to a type of cheap liquor common in Greece.

A shrewd negotiator and staunch supporter of the unity of the island under a federal umbrella, Clerides supports the demilitarisation of Cyprus and deployment of a multinational force in the event of a solution.
His administration takes credit for forging a common defence pact with Greece in November 1993, under which Athens would defend Cyprus in case of another Turkish move on the island.
"I will never surrender my country smaller (than what it is)," Clerides has said on numerous occasions, borrowing an ancient Greek oath.
Clerides and Denktash were friends years ago when both were studying law in London, but their relations cooled on returning to Cyprus.
Clerides came back to defend convicted guerrillas of the outlawed EOKA organisation who were seeking an end to British colonial rule in Cyprus.
Denktash went to the opposite camp, becoming crown prosecutor for the colonial administration.

"They are both very similar, actually," said one diplomat. "They both have the charisma. The only difference is Clerides sometimes opens his mouth and gets into trouble, while Denktash has been espousing the same old rhetoric for more than 30 years."
Born in Nicosia on April 24, 1919, Clerides was known as a daredevil Royal Air Force pilot whose Spitfire fighter was shot down over Germany in 1942 during a 1,000-bomber raid on Hamburg.
He was taken prisoner, escaped twice but was recaptured and remained interned until 1945.
The son of a prominent Nicosia lawyer, Clerides was called to the bar in London in 1951 and returned to Cyprus to take up law and help in the Eoka struggle.
He broke ranks with his father, Ioannis Clerides, who ran against Archbishop Makarios, the island's first president, in 1960. He became the first speaker of parliament after independence.

From 1968 Clerides had held the post of negotiator for the Greek Cypriot side in inter-communal talks with the Turkish Cypriots. But he resigned under pressure in 1976. He had also frequently represented his country at U.N. Security Council debates on the Cyprus problem.
As speaker of parliament, Clerides deputised for Makarios from July to December 1974, while Makarios was in exile following the coup.
His close relations with Makarios cooled when critics accused Clerides of overstepping his authority. He founded the right-wing Democratic Rally party in 1976, leading it from strength to strength.

Known for his sharp wit, unruffled personality and insistence on speaking old-fashioned "katharevousa" (literary) Greek which earned him suspensions from school as a teenager, Clerides has devoted the past 40 years to politics.
His wife, Lila-Irene, was born in India. They have one daughter, Kate, who is a member of the Cyprus parliament.
